title: Six feet of DNA fits inside one of your cells.
detail: The double helix is about 2 nanometers wide. Enlarge a typical nucleus to the size of a golf ball, and the DNA inside would stretch roughly 9 miles.

sources.label: NASA on the width of DNA

widgetText: Six feet of DNA fits in one cell.

title: You hear with bones your ancestors used to chew.
detail: The hammer and anvil in your ears evolved from bones that once formed a jaw joint. Today they vibrate when someone whispers.

sources.label: How jaw bones became ear bones

widgetText: Two ear bones used to help jaws chew.

title: Your nose carries broken copies of ancient smell genes.
detail: Humans have about 400 intact odor-receptor genes, dogs about 800, and African elephants nearly 2,000.
widgetText: Dogs have twice our smell-receptor genes.

title: The egg you grew from started forming inside your grandmother.
detail: While your mother was still a fetus, immature eggs were already forming in her ovaries. One of them eventually became the egg you grew from.

sources.label: Yale lectures on germ cell development

widgetText: Your egg began inside your grandmother.

title: You can see signs of your own white blood cells in a blue sky.
detail: Those tiny bright dots that dart across a clear blue sky can come from white blood cells moving through blood vessels in your eyes.

sources.label: Why bright dots move across a blue sky

widgetText: White blood cells make dots in a blue sky.

title: Your fingers became separate when the cells between them died.
detail: Early in development, your hand looked like a paddle. As cells in the webbing died away, individual fingers emerged.

sources.label: Programmed cell death and developing fingers

widgetText: Cells died to separate your fingers.

title: A Siamese cat’s fur is a heat map.
detail: Its skin makes more dark pigment in cooler spots. That’s why its ears, paws, and tail grow darker than its warm belly.

sources.label: UC Davis on temperature-sensitive coat color

widgetText: Siamese fur is a heat map.

title: You glow in the dark.
detail: Chemical reactions in your body release visible light about 1,000 times too faint for human eyes to see.

sources.label: Measuring visible light from the human body

widgetText: Your body gives off visible light.

title: There’s a hand inside a whale’s flipper.
detail: An X-ray reveals a wrist and rows of finger bones arranged much like yours.

sources.label: NOAA comparison of whale and human forelimbs

widgetText: A whale has fingers inside its flipper.

title: Two kernels on the same corn cob can have different dads.
detail: Each silk strand leads to one potential kernel and can catch pollen from a different plant.
widgetText: Corn kernels can have different dads.

title: Your DNA carries a broken recipe for vitamin C.
detail: Our ancestors could make it. One gene in the recipe stopped working, so humans now get vitamin C from food.

sources.label: The genetics of vitamin C loss

widgetText: We lost the ability to make vitamin C.

title: A wood frog’s heart can stop for the winter.
detail: As ice forms between its cells, its breathing and heartbeat stop. When the frog thaws, its heart starts beating again.
widgetText: A frozen wood frog’s heart can restart.

title: You’re reading through proteins your body made before you were born.
detail: Some proteins in the centers of your eye lenses stay with you for life.

sources.label: How the eye lens keeps its proteins

widgetText: Some eye proteins are older than you.

title: A mouse can read jellyfish DNA.
detail: Nearly all life shares the same genetic code. Given a jellyfish gene, mouse cells can make its fluorescent protein and glow green under blue light.

sources.label: How cells translate the genetic code

widgetText: A mouse can read jellyfish DNA.

title: The mushroom on your pizza is more closely related to you than to the tomato.
detail: Animals and fungi share a common ancestor that lived after the plant lineage branched off.

sources.label: Kew on the fungal family tree

widgetText: You’re kin to the mushroom on your pizza.

title: Tiny proteins are walking inside your cells.
detail: A protein called kinesin carries cargo along microscopic tracks, putting one molecular “foot” in front of the other.
widgetText: Tiny proteins walk inside your cells.

title: A moth can remember a smell it learned as a caterpillar.
detail: In one experiment, caterpillars learned to avoid a particular smell. They still avoided it after growing wings.
widgetText: A moth can remember being a caterpillar.

title: The carbon in a wooden chair used to float through the air.
detail: The tree took in carbon dioxide through its leaves and used that carbon to build the wood.

sources.label: US Forest Service on carbon in trees

widgetText: The carbon in wood came from the air.

title: A Venus flytrap counts while a bug walks on it.
detail: Two quick taps usually snap the trap shut. By the fifth signal, the plant starts making digestive enzymes.
widgetText: A Venus flytrap counts taps.

title: A sea slug can steal a sting from its lunch.
detail: After eating a sea anemone, it moves some of the unfired stinging capsules to the tips of the projections on its own back.

sources.label: Monterey Bay Aquarium on the opalescent nudibranch

widgetText: A sea slug can steal a sting.

title: You breathe out most of the fat you burn.
detail: When your body breaks down stored fat, about 84% of its mass leaves through your lungs as carbon dioxide. The rest becomes water.

sources.label: Where fat goes when it is used for energy

widgetText: You breathe out most of the fat you burn.

title: A single nerve cell can reach from your spine to your toes.
detail: Wiggle your big toe and part of the message travels down one long extension of a single cell.

sources.label: How far a motor neuron reaches

widgetText: One nerve cell can reach your toes.

title: One red blood cell can carry about a billion oxygen molecules.
detail: As it matures, the cell ejects its nucleus, leaving more room for the protein that carries oxygen.

sources.label: Red blood cells and oxygen capacity

widgetText: One red cell can carry a billion O₂ molecules.

title: One cell in your biceps can have thousands of nuclei.
detail: A muscle fiber starts as many small cells that fuse into one long cell and keep their nuclei.

sources.label: How a muscle fiber gains nuclei

widgetText: One muscle cell can have thousands of nuclei.

title: A tattoo can outlive the cells holding its ink.
detail: In mice, researchers watched fresh immune cells pick up pigment left behind by old ones. The ink stayed put through the handoff.
widgetText: A tattoo can outlive its ink-holding cells.

title: You have spinning turbines inside your cells.
detail: Inside your mitochondria, part of a protein called ATP synthase physically rotates as it makes ATP, the fuel your cells use.
widgetText: Tiny turbines spin inside your cells.

title: Your mitochondria have a family tree of their own.
detail: They descended from bacteria that took up residence inside another cell. They still carry their own DNA.

sources.label: The genetic systems of mitochondria and plastids

widgetText: Mitochondria have their own DNA.

title: Some of your immune cells cut and paste their own DNA.
detail: A developing B cell joins pieces of different DNA segments to build its own recipe for an antibody.
widgetText: Immune cells rearrange their own DNA.

title: Your parents could have shuffled their chromosomes more than 70 trillion ways.
detail: That’s just from which whole chromosomes the egg and sperm each inherit. Swapping pieces of chromosomes creates even more possibilities.
widgetText: Your parents had 70 trillion chromosome combos.

title: You can see genetics at work on a calico cat.
detail: Its orange and black patches show which of its two X chromosomes stayed active in the cells that color the fur.
widgetText: A calico’s patches reveal its active X.

title: A male honeybee has a grandfather but no father.
detail: He hatches from an unfertilized egg. His mother, the queen, had a father of her own.
widgetText: Male honeybees have no father.

title: Nine-banded armadillos usually have identical quadruplets.
detail: One fertilized egg splits into four embryos. A whole litter can share the same DNA in the way identical twins do.

sources.label: American Museum of Natural History on nine-banded armadillos

widgetText: One armadillo egg can become quadruplets.

title: Scientists discovered that DNA can jump by studying speckled corn.
detail: When a piece of DNA moves out of a pigment gene, a patch of cells can start making color again. That leaves a visible spot on the kernel.
widgetText: Speckled corn helped reveal jumping DNA.

title: Broccoli, kale, cabbage, and Brussels sprouts are all the same species.
detail: Generations of growers selected for different parts. With kale you eat the leaves. With broccoli you eat clusters of flower buds and their stalks.

sources.label: How one species became several vegetables

widgetText: Kale and broccoli are the same species.

title: A sunflower is a bouquet pretending to be one flower.
detail: Its center holds hundreds of tiny flowers. Each one can make a sunflower seed.

sources.label: The tiny flowers in a sunflower head

widgetText: One sunflower holds hundreds of flowers.

title: In Utah, you can walk through a grove of thousands of trunks and still be walking past the same tree.
detail: The aspen called Pando keeps sending up new trunks from a shared root system.
widgetText: Thousands of trunks can share one tree.

title: Scientists grew date palms from seeds about 2,000 years old.
detail: A female palm nicknamed Hannah grew from one ancient seed. Pollen from another ancient-seed palm helped her produce fresh dates.

sources.label: The first harvest from an ancient-seed date palm

widgetText: Ancient seeds grew palms bearing fresh dates.

title: The oxygen a leaf releases used to be part of water.
detail: During photosynthesis, the leaf splits water molecules. Some of those oxygen atoms pair up and float away as the gas you breathe.
widgetText: A leaf makes oxygen by splitting water.

title: Some bacteria grow tiny compasses inside themselves.
detail: They make chains of magnetic crystals that line up with Earth’s magnetic field as they swim.
widgetText: Some bacteria grow tiny compasses.

title: Some sea slugs eat algae and keep the parts that run on sunlight.
detail: They tuck the algae’s chloroplasts inside their own cells, where the stolen parts can keep photosynthesizing for months.
widgetText: Some sea slugs run partly on sunlight.

title: An octopus can taste what it touches.
detail: The suckers on its arms have chemical sensors, so reaching into a crack can give an octopus a taste of what’s hiding inside.
widgetText: Octopuses taste with their suckers.

title: Some Antarctic fish have nearly clear blood.
detail: Icefish lost the red protein hemoglobin. Oxygen travels dissolved directly in the liquid part of their blood.

sources.label: Comparing icefish blood with other fish blood

widgetText: Some Antarctic fish have clear blood.

title: Some sea stars send their stomach out for dinner.
detail: They pry a clam open just enough to slip their stomach inside and start digesting the meal in its own shell.

sources.label: How a sea star feeds on shellfish

widgetText: Sea stars slip their stomachs inside clams.

title: Some turtles can breathe through their butts.
detail: Australia’s Mary River turtle draws water into its rear opening, where specialized tissue absorbs oxygen.

sources.label: How Mary River turtles absorb oxygen underwater

widgetText: Some turtles take in oxygen through their rear.

title: Reindeer eyes change color with the seasons.
detail: The reflective layer at the back of the eye shifts from gold in summer to deep blue in winter.

sources.label: Why the backs of reindeer eyes change color

widgetText: Reindeer have seasonal color shifts in their eyes.

title: You and a giraffe have the same number of neck bones.
detail: You each have seven. A giraffe grows much longer versions of the same bones.
widgetText: You and a giraffe have seven neck bones.

title: We know the color of a dinosaur’s stripes.
detail: Microscopic pigment structures preserved in fossils suggest the feathery dinosaur Sinosauropteryx had a tail ringed in reddish brown and white.
widgetText: One dinosaur had a striped ginger tail.

title: Wombats make cube-shaped poop.
detail: Different parts of the intestine stretch by different amounts, shaping the corners before the poop comes out.
widgetText: Wombats make cube-shaped poop.

title: A wallaby can put a pregnancy on pause for about 11 months.
detail: A tammar wallaby can have one joey growing in her pouch while another waits as a tiny dormant embryo.

sources.label: Embryonic diapause in the tammar wallaby

widgetText: A wallaby can pause a pregnancy.

title: An axolotl regrowing a limb remembers where to start.
detail: Lose a hand at the wrist and it grows a hand. Lose the limb higher up and it rebuilds the missing arm, wrist, and fingers.

sources.label: How axolotl cells regrow the missing parts

widgetText: Axolotls can regrow just the missing parts.

title: One cell can unfold a neck 30 times its body length.
detail: The pond microbe Lacrymaria stores its extra surface in folds that open like origami when it hunts.
widgetText: One cell unfolds a neck 30 body lengths long.

title: One fruit fly makes sperm 20 times its own length.
detail: A single sperm cell from Drosophila bifurca can stretch about 2.3 inches.
widgetText: One fly makes sperm 20 times its length.

title: Cells from a pregnancy can stay for decades.
detail: Researchers found fetal cells circulating in one mother’s blood 27 years after she gave birth to her son.
widgetText: Fetal cells can stay in a mother for decades.

title: A whole stretch of seaweed can be one cell.
detail: Caulerpa grows feathery fronds and long runners that share one continuous cell filled with nuclei.
widgetText: A whole stretch of seaweed can be one cell.

title: Immune cells can catch bacteria in DNA nets.
detail: White blood cells called neutrophils release webs made of their own DNA and proteins.
widgetText: White blood cells can cast DNA nets.

title: Ancient chewing gum preserved a human genome.
detail: Someone chewed birch pitch about 5,700 years ago. Enough DNA stayed behind for scientists to reconstruct her genome.
widgetText: Ancient gum held a human genome.

title: Cold water changes how an octopus reads its genes.
detail: In the California two-spot octopus, nerve cells edit thousands of spots in RNA messages as temperatures change. Some edits alter the proteins those cells make.
widgetText: Cold changes how octopuses edit RNA.

title: One cell solves a 225,000-piece DNA puzzle.
detail: After mating, the pond organism Oxytricha stitches together more than 225,000 DNA segments to build a new working nucleus.
widgetText: One cell sorts 225,000 pieces of DNA.

title: An axolotl’s genome is about ten times the size of yours.
detail: One set of its chromosomes holds around 32 billion DNA letter pairs. Much of the extra length comes from repeated sequences.
widgetText: Axolotls carry ten times our DNA per set.

title: Your chromosome 2 still has a seam.
detail: Two ancestral chromosomes fused end to end. Scientists can still recognize traces of their old tips inside the joined chromosome.
widgetText: Human chromosome 2 has an ancient seam.

title: A mouse gene can tell a fly to grow a fly eye.
detail: In experiments, a mouse gene switched on the fly’s own eye-building instructions. The result was a compound eye like a fly’s.
widgetText: A mouse gene can switch on a fly eye.

title: A lungfish is more closely related to you than to a salmon.
detail: You and the lungfish share a common ancestor that lived after the salmon lineage branched off.
widgetText: A lungfish is closer kin to you than to salmon.

title: An ancient virus helped build the placenta you grew in.
detail: Humans inherited viral DNA that makes a protein called syncytin. It helps placental cells fuse together.
widgetText: Ancient viral DNA helps build the placenta.

title: Some insects get their color from ancient fungal genes.
detail: Pigment-making genes crossed from a fungus into an aphid ancestor. Its descendants still use them to make pigments, including one found in red pea aphids.
widgetText: Red aphids use pigment genes from fungi.

title: Some sea slug heads can grow a whole new body.
detail: Scientists saw sea slugs shed their bodies, heart included. Some of the surviving heads grew replacements.
widgetText: A sea slug head can regrow a heart.

title: Sleeping glassfrogs stash their blood.
detail: They pack nearly 90% of their circulating red blood cells into their liver, making the rest of the frog easier to see through.
widgetText: Glassfrogs hide red blood cells as they sleep.

title: A scallop can look back with up to 200 eyes.
detail: Each eye focuses light with a curved mirror made of tiny crystals, much like a reflecting telescope.
widgetText: Scallops can have up to 200 mirrored eyes.

title: An animal thawed from ancient permafrost had offspring.
detail: Researchers recovered a microscopic rotifer from Siberian ground dated to about 24,000 years ago. It became active and reproduced.
widgetText: A rotifer woke from ancient frozen ground.

title: A shark’s eyes keep a record of its age.
detail: Greenland sharks keep lens proteins made before birth. Carbon dating put one female’s age somewhere between 272 and 512 years.
widgetText: A shark’s eyes can reveal centuries of age.
